documents.title: Call: Unable to Eat, Worse Pain
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Wife called, then put patient on. For three or four days he can only get down a few spoonfuls before he is too full and nauseated to continue; mostly sips of water and part of a shake. Pain under the breastbone is worse and steady. Light-headed when he stands. He has not vomited. No black stools. Sugars 110-140, he took a smaller glargine dose last night. Endoscopy not until 1/22.

With early satiety, weight loss and now barely able to eat, I'm concerned about a narrowing at the stomach outlet and about dehydration. Advised ED today, wife will drive him. Called the ED to give them the background. Will follow.

events.reason: Upper abdominal pain, early satiety, poor intake, weight loss

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV and oral contrast, IV contrast given with IV hydration for reduced kidney function. The stomach is distended with retained fluid and food debris, and oral contrast has passed only slowly into the duodenum, suggesting delayed gastric emptying. There is focal narrowing of the distal stomach with circumferential wall thickening of the distal antrum and pylorus. No enlarged perigastric or regional lymph nodes. Liver without focal lesion. No ascites or peritoneal nodularity. Pancreas, spleen and adrenal glands unremarkable. Kidneys symmetric without hydronephrosis. Urinary bladder unremarkable. No bone lesions.
reports.conclusion: Distended stomach with retained contents suggesting delayed gastric emptying, with focal narrowing and wall thickening of the distal stomach at the pylorus. Endoscopy recommended. No lymphadenopathy or liver lesion.

reports.text: Specimen: stomach, pyloric channel, endoscopic biopsies (6 fragments). Microscopic: gastric mucosa infiltrated by malignant glands. Immunohistochemistry: HER2 1+ (negative). Mismatch repair proteins MLH1, PMS2, MSH2 and MSH6 retained (proficient). No Helicobacter organisms identified on immunostain.
reports.conclusion: Stomach, pylorus, biopsy: invasive adenocarcinoma. HER2 negative (IHC 1+). Mismatch repair proficient.

reports.text: CT of the chest with IV contrast for staging, given with IV hydration. Abdomen and pelvis imaged 01/09/2026. Lungs clear without nodules or consolidation. No pleural or pericardial effusion. No mediastinal, hilar or axillary lymphadenopathy. Heart normal in size.
reports.conclusion: No evidence of thoracic metastatic disease.

documents.title: Upper Endoscopy Report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
UPPER ENDOSCOPY (inpatient)
Date: 01/10/2026
Indication: delayed gastric emptying and distal gastric narrowing on CT; early satiety, nausea, weight loss; iron-deficiency anemia.
Sedation: MAC with propofol, airway protected after NG decompression.

Findings:
- Esophagus: normal.
- Stomach: moderate retained fluid and food debris, suctioned. Fundus and body normal on retroflexion. The pyloric channel is narrowed and the mucosa there is abnormal in appearance; the standard gastroscope passed with gentle pressure.
- Duodenum: bulb and second portion normal.

Biopsies: pyloric channel x6.

Impression: narrowed pyloric channel with abnormal mucosa, biopsied, suspicious for malignancy. Retained gastric contents.
Plan: await pathology; liquid diet as tolerated; surgical team following.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Discharge Summary: General Surgery
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL: GENERAL SURGERY DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 01/09/2026    Discharged: 01/14/2026
Patient: Philip Hall, 69 M    Allergies: NKDA

Principal diagnosis: adenocarcinoma of the stomach, pyloric region, with partial gastric outlet narrowing.
Secondary: mild iron-deficiency anemia; type 2 diabetes, long-standing and poorly controlled, with peripheral neuropathy and retinopathy; CKD stage 3b; neurogenic bladder; prior vitamin B12 deficiency on replacement; hypertension; hyperlipidemia.

History: referred from the ED. Several months of a dull, constant ache below the sternum that worsens with eating, so he has been eating less. Early fullness and intermittent nausea; he has not vomited recently, but over the few days before admission he could take only a few spoonfuls at a time. Roughly 15 lb unintentional weight loss over the last few months (76.0 kg on admission). Mother had gastric adenocarcinoma.

Exam on admission: mild epigastric tenderness without a palpable mass. Cardiopulmonary exam unremarkable. Neurologic: no focal deficit.

Workup:
- Labs: hemoglobin 11.2, MCV 78, ferritin 11, consistent with mild iron deficiency. Liver enzymes and bilirubin normal. Creatinine 1.79 (baseline per PCP records).
- CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast 1/9 (with IV hydration): distended stomach with retained contents suggesting delayed emptying, focal narrowing and wall thickening of the distal stomach at the pylorus; no lymphadenopathy, no liver lesions, no ascites.
- EGD 1/10: narrowed pyloric channel with abnormal mucosa, biopsied.
- Pathology 1/12: invasive adenocarcinoma; HER2 negative (1+); MMR proficient; no H. pylori.
- CT chest with contrast 1/12: no thoracic disease. Creatinine unchanged after contrast.

Hospital course: NPO with IV fluids and NG decompression for 24 hours, then clear and full liquids, then soft diet in small portions, tolerated without nausea by day 4. Insulin adjusted while intake was low; home glargine dose resumed once eating. Diagnosis discussed with patient and wife. Case presented at multidisciplinary tumor board planning; outpatient EUS arranged.

Discharge medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, insulin glargine 30 units nightly, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg IM monthly, NEW ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily.
Diet: soft, small frequent meals; vegan protein supplement shakes.
Follow-up: EUS 1/27; surgical oncology 2/3; PCP within 1 week.

General Surgery

documents.title: Post-discharge RN call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Spoke with pt and wife 2 days after discharge. Eating soft foods 5-6 small meals, keeping it down, nausea much less since the hospital. Mild ache after meals. Taking iron, other meds as before. Fasting sugars 120s-170s. Has his EUS date (1/27) and surgical oncology (2/3). Wife asked about protein shakes; reviewed vegan options with ~20 g protein. TCM visit confirmed for Monday 1/19.

documents.title: Transitional Care Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hospital follow-up (admitted 1/9-1/14, general surgery). Discharge summary, EGD, pathology and CT reports reviewed.

Summary: obstructing adenocarcinoma at the pylorus, HER2 negative, MMR proficient. Staging CT without nodes or distant spread. EUS 1/27, surgical oncology 2/3. Mild iron-deficiency anemia, on oral iron.

He and his wife are here together. He is quiet, says he "knew something was wrong." Thinking a lot about his mother's illness. Eating soft small meals 5-6 times a day without vomiting. Ache after eating persists but milder. No black stools. Fasting sugars 120s-180s. No lows.

Med reconciliation: metformin 1000 BID, glargine 30 qhs, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg IM monthly, ferrous sulfate 325 daily (new). Reviewed with wife.

Exam: thin, tired-appearing. Abdomen soft, mild epigastric tenderness. Heart regular, lungs clear.

A/P:
1. Gastric adenocarcinoma, localized on imaging. Next steps per surgery/GI. Answered questions about what EUS shows and what surgery might involve. He wants to proceed with treatment.
2. Nutrition: small frequent meals, protein shakes; weight next visit.
3. DM2: lower intake, watch for lows. If fasting under 100 twice, cut glargine to 24 and call.
4. Iron deficiency anemia: oral iron.
5. Neurogenic bladder: still not catheterizing; he denies leakage today. Reminded about urology.
Will see him for preoperative evaluation once surgery is scheduled.

documents.title: Endoscopic Ultrasound Report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
ENDOSCOPIC ULTRASOUND
Date: 01/27/2026
Indication: staging of biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the gastric pylorus.
Allergies: NKDA. Sedation: MAC.

Findings: radial and linear echoendoscope examination. Hypoechoic circumferential wall thickening at the pyloric channel. The lesion involves the muscularis propria without extension through the serosa. No perigastric, celiac or hepatoduodenal lymph nodes of concern. No ascites. Left lobe of the liver unremarkable from this view.

Impression: gastric adenocarcinoma of the pylorus, EUS stage uT2 N0.
Recommendations: findings to surgical oncology and tumor board.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Surgical Oncology Consultation
documents.author: surgical oncology
documents.body:
SURGICAL ONCOLOGY CONSULTATION
Visit: 02/03/2026
Re: Philip Hall, 69-year-old man

Dear Doctor,

Thank you for referring Mr. Hall with a newly diagnosed adenocarcinoma of the gastric pylorus causing partial outlet obstruction. Biopsy: invasive adenocarcinoma, HER2 negative, MMR proficient. CT abdomen/pelvis and chest: no nodal or distant disease. EUS: uT2 N0.

He is tolerating a soft diet in small portions. Weight has been stable since discharge. Comorbidities include long-standing type 2 diabetes with peripheral and autonomic neuropathy and retinopathy, CKD 3b (creatinine around 1.8), neurogenic bladder, hypertension and hyperlipidemia. NKDA. No prior abdominal surgery.

Exam: thin, no distress. Abdomen soft, mild epigastric tenderness, no palpable mass, no hernias.

Tumor board discussion (02/02/2026): localized cT2 N0 M0 distal gastric cancer with outlet narrowing. Perioperative chemotherapy was considered; given the obstruction, his pre-existing neuropathy and his kidney function, the board recommended upfront surgery, with adjuvant therapy decided on final pathology.

Plan:
- Staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings, then laparoscopic distal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and Roux-en-Y reconstruction if no peritoneal disease. Scheduled 02/17/2026.
- Risks, benefits and alternatives discussed with patient and wife; consent signed.
- Preoperative medical evaluation with you, please.
- Nutrition: continue protein supplements; dietitian visit before surgery.

Surgical Oncology

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 78. Normal axis and intervals. No ST or T-wave abnormality. Compared with 01/2022: no significant change.
reports.conclusion: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal ECG, unchanged.

documents.title: Preoperative Evaluation
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Preop eval for staging laparoscopy and laparoscopic distal gastrectomy, 2/17, surgical oncology.

Functional capacity: walks 20 minutes on flat ground, climbs a flight of stairs without stopping; >4 METs. No chest pain, no exertional dyspnea, no syncope. No history of heart disease, stroke or lung disease. Never smoker. No prior anesthesia. No bleeding problems.

Eating soft small meals, no vomiting. Weight stable since discharge.

Meds and allergies reconciled (NKDA).

Exam: thin. Airway unremarkable. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, mild epigastric tenderness. No edema.

ECG: normal, unchanged from 2022.
Labs today: CBC, BMP (creatinine 1.81).

Assessment: elevated-risk surgery; patient risk factors are insulin-treated diabetes and creatinine near 1.8 (RCRI 2 for the procedure plus comorbidities). Good functional capacity, no cardiac symptoms; no further cardiac testing needed.

Recommendations to surgical team:
- Hold metformin the day of surgery and until eating and creatinine stable after.
- Glargine: take 80% of usual (24 units) the night before; perioperative insulin per anesthesia.
- Hold lisinopril the morning of surgery.
- Continue atorvastatin.
- Avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxins; renally dose medications.
- Neurogenic bladder: may need a catheter postoperatively; voiding trial before removal.
- Hold oral iron 5 days around surgery.
Cleared from a medical standpoint.

reports.text: Specimen: distal stomach with attached omentum (distal gastrectomy), and separately submitted lymph node stations. Gross: ulcerated lesion at the pylorus. Microscopic: invasive adenocarcinoma invading the muscularis propria, not through it. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion identified. Proximal and distal margins negative. Lymph nodes: 0 of 27 involved. Peritoneal washings: negative for malignant cells.
reports.conclusion: Distal gastrectomy: invasive adenocarcinoma of the pylorus, pT2 N0 (0/27), margins negative. Peritoneal washings negative. AJCC pathologic stage IB.

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: surgical oncology
documents.body:
OPERATIVE REPORT
Date: 02/17/2026
Preoperative diagnosis: adenocarcinoma of the gastric pylorus, cT2 N0 M0, with outlet narrowing.
Postoperative diagnosis: same; no peritoneal disease.
Procedures: diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal washings; laparoscopic distal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy; Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy.
Anesthesia: general endotracheal.
Findings: no ascites, peritoneal implants or liver lesions. Tumor confined to the pyloric region, no serosal involvement visible. No enlarged nodes.
Estimated blood loss: 150 mL. Fluids: crystalloid. Urine: Foley placed after induction, clear urine.
Specimens: distal stomach and omentum; lymph node stations; washings.
Complications: none. Patient extubated and taken to PACU in stable condition.

Surgical Oncology

documents.title: Discharge Summary: Surgical Oncology
documents.author: surgical oncology
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admission: 02/17/2026  Discharge: 02/23/2026
Patient: Philip Hall, 69 M. NKDA.
Procedure: staging laparoscopy (washings negative), laparoscopic distal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and Roux-en-Y reconstruction, 02/17.

Course: uncomplicated. Diet advanced from clear liquids on POD 2 to soft small meals by POD 4. Pain controlled with acetaminophen and short-term low-dose oxycodone, off opioids by POD 4. Foley removed POD 2; given his neurogenic bladder, bladder scans were followed and he resumed intermittent self-catheterization in hospital before discharge, residuals acceptable after re-teaching. Glucose managed with basal-bolus insulin, home glargine resumed POD 3; metformin resumed at discharge with creatinine stable at baseline. Lisinopril resumed POD 3. Hemoglobin stable. Ambulating independently.

Final pathology (02/20): invasive adenocarcinoma of the pylorus, pT2 N0 (0/27 nodes), margins negative, washings negative. Stage IB.

Discharge medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, insulin glargine 30 units nightly, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily, cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg IM monthly; acetaminophen as needed.
Diet: post-gastrectomy diet, 6 small meals, separate liquids from solids.
Follow-up: surgical oncology 2 weeks; medical oncology 3/10; PCP within 1 week.

Surgical Oncology

documents.title: Post-discharge RN call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called day after discharge. Pt at home, wife present. Incisions dry, no redness or drainage. Pain 2-3/10 with acetaminophen. Eating small soft meals, mild fullness, no vomiting. Some loose stools after sweet drinks; reviewed post-gastrectomy diet (avoid sugary liquids, protein first). Fasting sugar this morning 132. Catheterizing at home since discharge without trouble. documents.title: Transitional Care Visit: After Gastrectomy
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM visit 4 days after discharge from distal gastrectomy (2/17). Operative note, discharge summary and final pathology reviewed with patient and wife: pT2 N0, 0/27 nodes, clear margins, stage IB. He was visibly relieved.

Doing OK. Six small meals, protein shakes twice daily. Fullness if he eats too fast. A few loose stools after juice, better since stopping it. Pain minimal, acetaminophen at night only. Walking the hallway and driveway. Catheterizing four times daily again since the hospital. Sugars 120s-180s fasting, no lows.

Meds reconciled: metformin 1000 BID, glargine 30 qhs, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, ferrous sulfate 325 daily, cyanocobalamin monthly, acetaminophen prn.

Exam: weight 72.6 kg. Laparoscopic port sites and small extraction incision healing, no erythema or drainage. Abdomen soft, appropriately tender near incisions. Heart regular, lungs clear.

A/P:
1. S/p distal gastrectomy for stage IB gastric adenocarcinoma: recovering well. Med onc 3/10.
2. Nutrition/weight: down ~3 kg since surgery, expected. Dietitian follow-up through surgery program.
3. B12: continue monthly IM, now more important after gastrectomy. Iron: continue, CBC in April.
4. DM2: continue current doses, watch for lows with small meals.
5. Neurogenic bladder: good that he's catheterizing again; encouraged him to keep it up and see urology.
RTC April.

orders.order: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast, surveillance at 6 months

documents.title: Medical Oncology Consultation
documents.author: medical oncology
documents.body:
MEDICAL ONCOLOGY CONSULTATION
Visit date: 03/10/2026
Re: Philip Hall, 69 M, retired postal worker

Dear Doctor,

We met Mr. Hall and his wife to discuss treatment after resection of a gastric adenocarcinoma of the pylorus. He underwent laparoscopic distal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and Roux-en-Y reconstruction on 02/17/2026 following negative staging laparoscopy. Pathology: pT2 N0 (0/27 nodes), R0, no lymphovascular or perineural invasion; HER2 negative, MMR proficient. AJCC stage IB.

He is recovering well, eating six small meals a day. ECOG 1. Comorbid diabetes with neuropathy, CKD 3b, neurogenic bladder on intermittent catheterization. NKDA.

Exam: thin, well-healing incisions, abdomen soft, no hepatomegaly, no supraclavicular nodes.

Assessment and recommendation: after upfront D2 resection with an adequate node count and no high-risk features, adjuvant chemotherapy or chemoradiation is not expected to add meaningful benefit for pT2 N0 disease, and his pre-existing neuropathy and kidney function would add risk. We recommend surveillance.

Surveillance plan: visits every 3-6 months for 2 years, then every 6-12 months to year 5. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast (with IV hydration) every 6 months for 2 years; first scan in August. Lifelong B12 replacement (already on monthly injections) and periodic iron studies after gastrectomy.

Medical Oncology

documents.title: eating question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Good morning. Since the operation I get sweaty and shaky about half an hour after I eat if I eat too quickly, then it goes away. Sugar was 168 when I checked once during it. Is this normal? Philip

documents.title: RE: eating question
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Hi Mr. Hall, I reviewed this with the doctor. Feeling sweaty and shaky soon after eating, with a normal or high sugar, is common in the first months after this surgery when food moves into the intestine quickly. It usually settles with: eating slowly, smaller portions, protein and fat with each meal, and drinking liquids 30 minutes before or after rather than with food. Avoid juice and sweets. Your sugar of 168 means it is not a low. If you ever feel this way with a sugar under 70, treat it and call us. Your surgery dietitian can also help.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up: Diabetes, Post-gastrectomy
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Two months after distal gastrectomy. Med onc 3/10: surveillance only, no chemo, CT in August. Letter reviewed.

Eating better, six small meals, the after-meal sweaty spells are rare now that he eats slowly. Weight about steady. Fasting sugars 130s-190s. No lows. Energy improving, walking 20-30 minutes. B12 shots monthly, iron daily.

Exam: weight 71.8 kg. Incisions healed. Abdomen soft, nontender. Heart regular, lungs clear. Feet: skin intact, monofilament reduced at toes.

A/P:
1. DM2: A1c 8.9 drawn today. Not the time to push intensification while his eating is still settling; continue metformin 1000 BID and glargine 30, recheck in summer.
2. Gastric cancer stage IB, s/p resection: surveillance per oncology.
3. Iron deficiency anemia: CBC today, continue iron.
4. CKD 3b: BMP today.
5. HTN: BP lower since weight loss, fine on lisinopril 20.
RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Your labs from yesterday
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Philip, A1c is 8.9. Kidney function is the same as before surgery (creatinine 1.80). Hemoglobin is still low, a bit below February's value; keep taking the iron every day and we'll recheck in the summer. Glad the eating is going better.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Regional hospital ED. Seen 07/12/2026.
Patient: Philip Hall, 69 M. Allergies: NKDA.

Chief complaint: constant leaking of urine, can't empty bladder.

HPI: 69-year-old man with neurogenic bladder first evaluated by urology in 2024, long-standing poorly controlled type 2 diabetes with peripheral neuropathy, and gastric adenocarcinoma diagnosed this year (distal gastrectomy in February). For about four months he has had constant dribbling of urine, including after he voids, and a persistent sense that the bladder is not empty. He is changing his underwear several times a day and the symptoms have slowly worsened. Despite going to the bathroom frequently he never feels relieved. No burning, no blood in the urine, no suprapubic pain. His wife adds that he often struggles to get started and there can be a long wait before a good stream comes. When asked, he acknowledges past episodes of retention for which he used intermittent catheterization; he stopped some time ago.

Meds (per patient list): metformin 1000 mg BID, insulin glargine 30 units at bedtime, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, retired postal worker.
Family: father with type 2 diabetes; mother with gastric adenocarcinoma; maternal grandfather with colon cancer.

Exam: well-appearing, afebrile. Abdomen soft, nontender; a mass is palpable in the lower abdomen consistent with a distended bladder. Healed laparoscopic incisions. DRE: smooth prostate of normal size, no nodules. Neuro: decreased sensation in the feet and legs consistent with his diabetic neuropathy; strength intact.

Results: HbA1c 9.2%. BMP: creatinine 1.76, at his known baseline; no acute kidney injury; electrolytes unremarkable. Urinalysis negative for infection and blood.
Bedside bladder ultrasound after voiding: post-void residual 450 mL, significant retention.

ED course: 16 Fr Foley catheter placed with return of clear urine; patient comfortable afterward.

Impression: chronic urinary retention with overflow incontinence from known neurogenic bladder; not infected; renal function at baseline.
Disposition: discharged home with Foley and leg bag, catheter care teaching done. Urology follow-up within 1 week for voiding trial. PCP follow-up in 1-2 days. Return for fever, catheter blockage, blood in urine or abdominal pain.

Emergency Medicine

documents.title: Post-ED RN call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: ED record received this morning (urinary retention with overflow, PVR 450, Foley placed). Called pt: Foley draining clear yellow urine into leg bag, no pain, no fever. Wife emptying night bag fine. Urology appointment 7/21 booked by ED. Visit with PCP tomorrow at 2:40.

documents.title: ED Follow-up: Urinary Retention
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ED record 7/12 reviewed: overflow incontinence from neurogenic bladder, PVR 450, Foley placed, creatinine 1.76 (his baseline), UA clean, A1c 9.2.

He tells me he stopped catheterizing again a few weeks after the surgery, around March, because it felt like too much on top of everything. The leaking started not long after and he was embarrassed to bring it up in April. Since the Foley, he is dry and comfortable. No fever, no flank pain.

Exam: afebrile. Abdomen soft, nontender, bladder not palpable. Foley secured to thigh, draining clear urine. Heart regular, lungs clear.

A/P:
1. Neurogenic bladder with chronic retention and overflow, off CIC since March. Urology 7/21 for voiding trial; most likely he will need to go back to self-catheterization, and we talked about how to make that sustainable (fewer, scheduled times, wife's help with supplies). Catheter care reviewed.
2. DM2: A1c 9.2. With his eating stable now, I raised adding a medicine again; he wants to get the bladder sorted first. Next visit in September.
3. CKD 3b: stable.
4. Gastric cancer: CT in August per oncology.

documents.title: Urology Follow-up Letter
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY
Visit: 07/21/2026
Re: Philip Hall, DOB 07/22/1956

Dear Doctor,

Mr. Hall was seen after his 07/12 ED visit for retention with overflow (PVR 450 mL), his first urology visit since 05/2024. He had stopped clean intermittent catheterization in 2025, restarted it after his February gastrectomy, then stopped again in March.

Voiding trial: Foley removed this morning, bladder backfilled. He voided small amounts with straining. Post-void residual by bladder scan 410 mL.

Assessment: neurogenic bladder from diabetic autonomic neuropathy with chronic retention; failed voiding trial.
Plan: clean intermittent catheterization five times daily, re-taught today with good technique; catheter supplies reordered (new prior authorization will be requested). Avoid anticholinergics. Return in 6 weeks with a catheter volume diary, sooner for fever or hematuria.

NKDA.

Urology

MEDICAL ONCOLOGY FOLLOW-UP
Visit 08/18/2026
Re: Philip Hall, 70 M

Six months after distal gastrectomy for stage IB (pT2 N0) adenocarcinoma of the pylorus. He feels well, eating small frequent meals, weight steady since spring. No abdominal pain, vomiting or dysphagia. Back on intermittent catheterization after an ED visit for urinary retention in July.

Exam: no supraclavicular nodes, abdomen soft and nontender, incisions well healed.

CT chest/abdomen/pelvis 08/14/2026: postsurgical change, no recurrence or metastasis.

Plan: continue surveillance. Next visit and CT in February 2027. Continue B12 and iron; we will check iron studies with his next labs.

documents.title: CT scan
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hello doctor, the cancer doctor said the CT scan was clear. My wife wanted me to ask you also, so we hear it twice. Also see you in September. Philip

documents.title: RE: CT scan
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Philip, yes, I read the report too: no sign of the cancer coming back, and the surgery site looks as it should. That's very good news. Next scan in February. We'll go over the diabetes and the bladder at your visit on September 10th.
